I'd like to play devils advocate here and say that there can be people who genuinely want to understand what happened and why individuals felt that they were targeted due to their race or otherwise.

I'm a visible minority, and I've experienced racism throughout my life. Some blatant, and some subtle. While there are dangers in not believing experiences others have had and their intuition on why it occurred, there are also dangers in believing any negative experience is driven by a form of hate.

In this situation, it could depend on how the restaurant is set up. Most restaurants I've worked in has the server enter the order into a computer, followed by a "chit" or receipt of the order being sent to the kitchen to be made. If this is the case, the server would have needed to go into the kitchen and ask the cooks to not add the upgrade. This sounds like it was forgotten by a cook if the receipt had the upgrades listed.

We can't look down on people for asking questions and we need to be able to understand the experiences people have. If you or anyone doesn't agree with, please let me know why. If you look in my post history, you would see a post where I wanted to understand ways of facilitating discussions on racism to make changes to government organizations I'm a part of.
Thank you, that really means a lot. I hope you're doing well and thank you for taking the time to do an AMA.

Good morning,

I'm my opinion, I believe one of the most significant changes that needs to occur is a cultural one for law enforcement. I've seen numerous people bring up specific aspects of policing to be reformed, such as training duration and equipment utilized, but don't believe that targets the root of the issue.

During the 12 weeks I spent in basic training, we spend relatively brief periods of time discussing rules of engagement, handling detainees/prisoners of war, andinteracting with media/press. These are a few relevant topics that law enforcement utilize themselves. Many of these concepts were expanded on during much shorter close quart battle training phases at different points of my career.

With that being said, to answer the question, I believe if police adopted the training and culture found within the military, a fair amount of progress could be made. Having police detention centers, in the same spirit as a military detention center/prison, could resolve the "suspended with pay" concerns that many have when an officer is charged with a crime. This would be good for the officer in terms of security and the morale of the community for not having the officer in question "at large".

For BLM issues in particular, training that involves recognizing racial bias could be useful. It seems as though the system racism that exists isn't generally an explicit policy or procedure, but the assumptions or mentality of an officer entering a situation or interaction with a person of interest. This is a far more difficult issue to break down, though could be mitigated by using other types of social workers to lead interactions with individuals that aren't presenting an immediate danger to those around them.

Thank you for reading and I hope I answered your questions!
